## Start here

This project studies patterns of constructive, destructive, and *laissez-faire*
leadership in Chilean salaried workers and hospital workers. It accompanies a
manuscript being prepared for *International Archives of Occupational and
Environmental Health*.

The project has **two primary questions**:

1. Which leadership profiles can be identified in the general salaried-worker
   survey, and why retain a four-class solution?
2. Can the same item-response profiles describe workers in both the general and
   hospital samples, and how does their prevalence differ between settings?

Characteristics and covariate associations are secondary questions. The hospital
comparison is a primary part of the study. Sensitivity analyses address specific
alternative modeling choices after those primary questions have been examined.

**Choose how to read.** Follow the numbered reports below for the scientific
argument. Open the accompanying `.qmd` source to inspect how a result was produced.
Use [the export guide](EXPORTS.md) to find the underlying tables and reusable
objects. The [repository README](README.md) gives a shorter starting point.

::: {.callout-note title="What this directory establishes"}
The main report and its aggregate exports were refreshed on September 7, 2026,
using the saved measurement estimates. The multiple-group and Part 2 sources
received export-only updates, but their linked HTML files remain snapshots of
earlier runs; their new exports will be written at their next render. The other
linked reports are also saved snapshots. Their tables
and output were reviewed for participant-level records before inclusion in the
public-file allowlist. Check each report's execution settings, class labels,
diagnostics, and session information together with the relevant export manifest.
This page itself runs no statistical analysis.
:::

## Read the analyses in this order

### 1. Identify and characterize the leadership profiles

[Read the main report](leadership_LCA_analysis.html) ·
[Inspect the source](leadership_LCA_analysis.qmd)

Begin with the measurement model. The analysis uses 13 items from the 14-item
Constructive-Destructive Leadership Scale. Item 3 is excluded because its wording
was administered incorrectly. Responses retain four ordered categories. Sex is
included as a concomitant in this general-sample measurement model.

Read the enumeration table and profile plots together: an information criterion,
classification quality, minimum class size, and interpretability answer different
parts of the selection question. The retained four-class model is then used for
weighted characteristics, classification diagnostics, three-step associations,
marginal predicted probabilities, and a comparison of modal and BCH estimates.

**Find a number:** [enumeration](table1_enumeration.csv),
[full Table 2](table2_full_13item.csv),
[class counts and weighted shares](table2_class_sizes_13item.csv),
[item-response probabilities](table3_itemprob.csv), and
[classification diagnostics](table_classification_diagnostics.csv).
The [export guide](EXPORTS.md) describes the new numeric and provenance exports.

### 2. Evaluate the shared profiles across settings

[Read the multiple-group report](leadership_LCA_multigroup_hospital.html) ·
[Inspect the source](leadership_LCA_multigroup_hospital.qmd)

This is the second primary axis. The report harmonizes the same 13 items between
the two samples, compares shared and setting-specific item-response probabilities,
and examines profile prevalence by setting. Separate within-setting fits provide
additional context for the shared-profile interpretation.

**Reading key:** measurement invariance concerns the profiles' item-response
probabilities. It does not require equal class prevalences. The information
criteria can disagree; inspect the complete comparison rather than interpreting
one favorable criterion as proof that all measurement differences are absent.
For the reported differences, the convention is **free minus invariant**: a
positive difference in BIC favors the invariant model.

**Find a number:** [sample accounting](mg_sample_sizes.csv). The full invariance
comparison and group-specific prevalences are presented in the report.

### 3. Compare associations between the two samples

[Read Part 2](leadership_LCA_analysis_part2_sample_comparison.html) ·
[Inspect the source](leadership_LCA_analysis_part2_sample_comparison.qmd)

Part 2 uses the shared four-class measurement model to compare covariate
associations on a common profile scale. It includes both one-covariate-at-a-time
ML three-step models and, in Section 5, a mutually adjusted model with eight
covariates. The latter includes seven binary covariates and job satisfaction,
standardized within each sample.

**Reading key:** an OR compares a profile with its specified reference within a
sample. A ratio of odds ratios (ROR) compares that association between samples:
the direction here is **hospital OR divided by general-sample OR**. Read the
confidence intervals, multiplicity results, and model diagnostics with the point
estimates. The surveys are anonymous, so partial participant overlap cannot be
excluded when interpreting cross-sample uncertainty.

**Find a number:** [numeric unadjusted ROR table](tableS7_ror_values.csv) and
[formatted unadjusted ROR table](tableS7_ror_formatted.csv). For the adjusted
eight-covariate comparisons, use Section 5 of the report; Table S7 exports belong
to the preceding one-covariate-at-a-time models.

### 4. Examine adjustment within the general sample

[Read Part 3](leadership_LCA_analysis_part3_or_adjusted.html) ·
[Inspect the source](leadership_LCA_analysis_part3_or_adjusted.qmd)

Part 3 compares unadjusted and mutually adjusted ML three-step ORs using the saved
general-sample measurement model. It also reports covariate correlations and
collinearity diagnostics. The actual adjustment set contains eight covariates.

**Reading key:** this report uses the general-sample model, whereas Part 2 uses a
shared multiple-group model. In Part 3, the job-satisfaction OR is per one score
point; in Part 2's adjusted model, it is per within-sample standard deviation.
Those coefficients should not be compared as if their units or measurement
models were identical. The reference profile is identified from the fitted
profiles; check the report's label and the export filename together.

**Find a number:** [numeric unadjusted and adjusted ORs, reference C3](tableUA_or_values_refC3.csv).

### 5. Check uncertainty about the number of classes

[Read the five- and eight-class sensitivity report](leadership_LCA_8class_sensitivity.html) ·
[Inspect the source](leadership_LCA_8class_sensitivity.qmd)

Despite its filename, this notebook covers both eight- and five-class solutions.
It examines alternatives motivated by the information criteria, compares their
profiles with the retained four-class solution, and studies whether the more
detailed partition changes the substantive interpretation.

**Reading key:** distinguish additional subdivisions of a broad profile from a
substantively different pattern. This notebook performs measurement-model fits;
it is not a display-only transformation of the retained four-class object.

### 6. Examine the role of job satisfaction in adjustment

[Read the seven-covariate sensitivity report](leadership_LCA_part2_adjusted_nojobsat.html) ·
[Inspect the source](leadership_LCA_part2_adjusted_nojobsat.qmd)

This notebook inherits selected code chunks from Part 2 and compares the
cross-sample adjusted models with and without job satisfaction. It keeps the
shared measurement model and the other seven covariates, allowing the change in
the adjustment set to be examined directly.

**Reading key:** the comparison shows how estimates depend on conditioning on job
satisfaction. It does not establish a temporal or causal role for that variable
in these cross-sectional data.

**Find a number:** [seven-covariate estimates](table4_adjusted_nojobsat_values.csv)
and [eight-versus-seven-covariate comparison](table4_adjusted_8vs7_comparison.csv).

### 7. Trace the publication figures to their saved inputs

[Read the consolidated figure report](Figures_IAOEH_consolidated.html) ·
[Inspect the source](Figures_IAOEH_consolidated.qmd)

This notebook prepares the four manuscript figures from saved results:
enumeration, general-sample item-response probabilities, shared invariant
profiles, and setting-specific prevalence. Figure 1 also uses adjacent-solution
agreement where the required enumeration assignments are available. Its checks
connect those assignments to the fitted enumeration results.

**Reading key:** the consolidated Figure 3 depicts shared profiles from the
invariant model. It is different from the separately fitted profile comparison
shown in the multiple-group report. Match the figure to the model named in its
caption.

## Understand the quantities before comparing them

| Quantity | What it represents | Where to check |
|---|---|---|
| Analytic `n` | Actual participants included after the stated eligibility and missing-data filters | Sample accounting and class-count exports |
| Weighted class share | Share of the modal classification after applying survey weights | Table 2 class-size export |
| Model-estimated class prevalence | Prevalence obtained from the specified latent-class model | Measurement-model output and profile figures |
| Weighted median and Q1–Q3 | The continuous characteristic's weighted distribution within a modal class | Full Table 2 and numeric summary exports |
| Table 2 P-value | A global comparison across the four modal classes, using the available survey design | Test-details export described in the export guide |
| Table 2 SMD | Maximum absolute standardized mean difference across class pairs, using weighted moments | Pairwise export described in the export guide |
| Three-step OR | A covariate association accounting for classification error through the specified estimator | Model-specific association report |

Counts, weighted shares, and model-estimated prevalence are distinct quantities.
A P-value alongside a median is based on a distributional/rank comparison, while
the conventional SMD uses means and variances. Neither should be read as a
standardized difference between medians. General-sample descriptives use survey
weights; hospital analyses use weight 1 where no sampling weight is available.
The currently available general-sample design is weights-only, so its variance
estimates do not reconstruct unprovided clustering or stratification variables.

## Reproduce the workflow

### Inputs and software

Run commands from the project directory with R and Quarto installed. Each analysis
notebook declares its required R packages and prints session information. Record
those versions with a released set of outputs; installing a package today does
not guarantee the same version used in an earlier report.

The private input files used by the current sources are:

- General survey: `BD_2020_input3_match_not_miss.rds`.
- Hospital survey: `Base de datos 27.8.2019.dta`.

The main, multiple-group and Part 2 notebooks accept `LCA_RAW_PATH`; the latter
two also accept `LCA_HOSPITAL_PATH`. They check project-local defaults before
legacy locations. The remaining notebooks retain their own
`load-data` configuration, including existing Google Drive paths. Configure
those paths to point to the authorized local data before running them on another
computer. Setting `LCA_RAW_PATH` for the main notebook does not automatically
configure every downstream source.

### Main-table refresh using the existing measurement results

```powershell
quarto render leadership_LCA_analysis.qmd
```

The main notebook reuses compatible saved measurement results when available,
validates their correspondence with the analysis data, and updates the
descriptive and downstream exports. If no usable saved results exist, a complete
measurement run is required. This is why a table refresh and a complete
replication can have very different running times.

For a deliberate fresh measurement fit:

```powershell
$env:LCA_REFIT = "1"
quarto render leadership_LCA_analysis.qmd
Remove-Item Env:\LCA_REFIT
```

### Full analysis order

The following order produces the main inputs before their consumers. It includes
measurement fits and secondary association fits; it is not needed merely to read
the saved reports or rebuild this index.

```powershell
$env:LCA_REFIT = "1"
$env:LCA_FINAL = "1"
quarto render leadership_LCA_analysis.qmd
Remove-Item Env:\LCA_REFIT
quarto render leadership_LCA_multigroup_hospital.qmd
quarto render leadership_LCA_analysis_part2_sample_comparison.qmd
quarto render leadership_LCA_analysis_part3_or_adjusted.qmd
quarto render leadership_LCA_8class_sensitivity.qmd
quarto render leadership_LCA_part2_adjusted_nojobsat.qmd
quarto render Figures_IAOEH_consolidated.qmd
Remove-Item Env:\LCA_FINAL
quarto render index.qmd
```

The no-job-satisfaction notebook can create `cache_g4_inv_part2.rds`, which the
consolidated figures consume. Part 2 can also read dated `part2_cache_*.rds`
objects. Verify that any reused cache matches the intended data, item coding,
and estimation settings; `LCA_FINAL` does not by itself certify an older cache.
Some notebooks permit execution to continue after an error, so inspect the
rendered diagnostics as well as the final output-created message.

### Build only this directory

```powershell
quarto render index.qmd
```

This command needs no participant data and does not run the linked notebooks.
Relative report links work when the HTML reports are kept beside `index.html`.
The source links remain usable when the `.qmd` files are included alongside them.

## Reuse outputs and prepare a public repository

The [export guide](EXPORTS.md) defines the distinction between public aggregate
results and private reusable objects. For new notebooks, use
[the results loader](R/load_leadership_results.R) and the documented schema
instead of extracting rounded numbers from an HTML table. The
[Table 2 implementation](R/leadership_table2.R) exposes the descriptive and
comparison calculations.

`lca_results.rds` is a **private analysis bundle**: it contains participant-level
posterior probabilities and may contain aligned analysis data and fitted objects.
The same applies to enumeration assignments, fitted-model caches, and raw survey
files. These are not public aggregate tables. The separate
`lca_results_public.rds` contains aggregate results; `output_manifest.csv` records
export checksums so a released file can be tied to a producing run.

For GitHub, publish the sources, this guide, the export documentation, and the
reviewed aggregate tables, figures, and reports that belong to the same release.
Inspect reports for embedded individual records or local-path information before
publishing. Keep participant-containing files and caches outside the public
release. Individual-level data are confidential and cannot be made publicly
available. The investigators permit public release of aggregate results only.

A reader with only the public release can inspect the calculations and compare
reported numbers with aggregate exports. A researcher with authorized input data
can additionally rerun the analyses. GitHub renders the README and source files;
the rendered HTML reports need a website host such as GitHub Pages to open as
webpages. A repository URL and site deployment can be added once selected.

Older NAQ, alcohol, Stata, and *poLCA* materials in the working folder are
historical research files. They are outside the current leadership-manuscript
reading path and should not be mistaken for its final analytical pipeline.
